topics.title: Volatility 3 Command Syntax and Usage
topics.content: Volatility 3 is a complete rewrite of the Volatility memory forensics framework, designed for Python 3 with improved performance and modularity. The basic command structure is: vol -f <memory_dump> <plugin>. Unlike Volatility 2, you no longer need to specify a profile - Volatility 3 uses symbol tables (ISF files) and autodetects the operating system. The framework supports multiple memory formats including raw dumps, crash dumps, hibernation files, VMware snapshots (.vmem), VirtualBox core dumps, and LiME format for Linux. Key flags include: -f for specifying the memory file, -o for output directory, -r for renderer selection (quick, json, csv, pretty), --single-location for specific offset analysis, and -v for verbose output. Volatility 3 plugins are namespaced by OS: windows.*, linux.*, and mac.*. You can list all available plugins with 'vol --help' or 'vol -f dump.mem windows. --help' for Windows-specific plugins. The framework automatically downloads required symbol tables from the Volatility symbol server, though you can specify custom symbol paths with --symbol-dirs. For large memory dumps (16GB+), consider using the --cache option to speed up repeated analysis. Output can be redirected to files using standard shell redirection or the built-in renderers for JSON/CSV export.

warnings: Memory dumps can be very large (8GB-128GB), ensure sufficient disk space for both the dump and extracted artifacts
Some plugins require symbol tables - Volatility 3 auto-downloads from Microsoft symbol server but this requires internet access
Always verify dump integrity with windows.info before deep analysis - corrupted dumps produce unreliable results
Running multiple plugins simultaneously can consume significant RAM - monitor system resources
best_practices: Always run windows.info first to understand the memory image OS version and verify it loaded correctly
Use -r json for machine-parseable output when scripting or integrating with other tools
Save all outputs to files with timestamps - memory forensics requires documentation for court admissibility
Run initial triage plugins first: pslist, pstree, netscan, malfind, cmdline
Use --offline flag when working in air-gapped environments to prevent symbol download attempts
For repeated analysis, use --cache-path to speed up subsequent runs

topics.title: Memory Acquisition Methods
topics.content: Before using Volatility, you need a memory image. Memory acquisition is the process of capturing the contents of RAM while preserving volatile evidence. For Windows, popular tools include: WinPmem (open-source, supports multiple output formats), FTK Imager (AccessData, GUI-based, widely accepted in court), DumpIt (single executable, no installation), Belkasoft RAM Capturer (free, portable), and Magnet RAM Capture. For Linux, LiME (Linux Memory Extractor) is the standard, compiled as a kernel module that dumps memory to file or network. For macOS, osxpmem or MacQuisition are used. Memory formats supported by Volatility 3 include: raw/dd format (simple memory dump), Microsoft crash dumps (.dmp), hibernation files (hiberfil.sys), VMware snapshots (.vmem), VirtualBox core dumps, QEMU memory dumps, and LiME format (.lime). When acquiring memory, time is critical - RAM is volatile and changes constantly. Minimize interaction with the target system, use trusted acquisition tools from a USB drive, and document the acquisition process including timestamps, hash values, and chain of custody. For live forensics, consider that the acquisition tool itself will appear in memory. Remote acquisition is possible using tools like F-Response or Velociraptor.

warnings: Memory acquisition itself modifies memory - the acquisition tool loads into RAM
Never install acquisition tools on the target system - run from USB or network share
Hibernation files contain memory from hibernation time, not current state
Virtual machine snapshots may not capture all memory regions accurately
Encrypted memory (AMD SME/SEV, Intel TME) may prevent successful acquisition
best_practices: Use acquisition tools from a known-good, write-protected USB drive
Calculate and record hash values (MD5/SHA1/SHA256) immediately after acquisition
Document everything: time, date, tool version, system state, analyst name
Acquire memory before disk - memory is more volatile
For VMs, prefer native snapshot/suspend over in-guest acquisition when possible
Maintain chain of custody documentation for legal proceedings

topics.title: Symbol Tables and ISF Files
topics.content: Volatility 3 uses Intermediate Symbol Format (ISF) files instead of the profile system from Volatility 2. ISF files are JSON representations of operating system debugging symbols that tell Volatility the memory layout of kernel structures like EPROCESS, KTHREAD, and other critical data structures. For Windows analysis, Volatility downloads PDB files from the Microsoft Symbol Server and converts them to ISF format. The symbols are stored in a local cache (typically ~/.volatility3/symbols or %USERPROFILE%/.volatility3/symbols on Windows). For Linux and macOS, you may need to generate custom symbols using the dwarf2json tool against a kernel with debugging symbols. The symbol files are critical - without correct symbols, Volatility cannot parse memory structures and plugins will fail or return incorrect data. Common issues include: symbol download failures (firewall/proxy blocks), mismatched symbols (wrong OS version), and missing symbols for custom/patched kernels. You can specify additional symbol directories with --symbol-dirs and use --offline to prevent network symbol downloads. For enterprise environments, consider hosting an internal symbol mirror.

topics.title: Process Enumeration with pslist, pstree, psscan
topics.content: Process enumeration is fundamental to memory forensics. Volatility 3 provides three complementary plugins for process discovery. PsList walks the ActiveProcessLinks doubly-linked list in EPROCESS structures - this is how the OS tracks running processes. PsTree presents processes hierarchically showing parent-child relationships, essential for understanding process spawning patterns. PsScan uses pool tag scanning to find EPROCESS structures in memory, including terminated and unlinked (hidden) processes. The key insight: rootkits often use Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) to unlink processes from the ActiveProcessLinks list while keeping them running. Such hidden processes appear in PsScan but not PsList. Comparing outputs reveals hidden malware. When analyzing output, examine: suspicious process names (misspellings like 'svch0st.exe'), unusual parent-child relationships (cmd.exe spawning from explorer.exe is normal, from services.exe is suspicious), processes with no parent (orphaned), processes in unusual sessions, single-threaded svchost.exe (normally multi-threaded), and processes with abnormal handle counts. Timestamp analysis reveals timeline - processes started at system boot vs. during user session vs. at unusual hours.

Compare session IDs - malware in session 0 (services) vs session 1 (user) behaves differently
Look for processes with unusual thread counts or handle patterns

topics.title: Command Line Analysis with cmdline
topics.content: The cmdline plugin extracts command line arguments for each process, revealing how processes were launched and with what parameters. This is critical for malware analysis as attackers often pass encoded commands, download URLs, or configuration parameters via command line. The plugin reads the PEB (Process Environment Block) structure to extract the full command line string. Key things to look for: encoded PowerShell commands (base64 -enc, -e, -EncodedCommand), curl/wget downloading malware, unusual script interpreters (wscript, cscript, mshta), processes launched from temp directories, regsvr32/rundll32 with remote URLs (Living off the Land), net/sc/schtasks for persistence, and any obfuscated or unusually long command lines. Process Hollowing and injection attacks may show legitimate process names but with suspicious command lines. Compare command lines against known-good baselines - svchost.exe should always have a -k parameter, for example. Empty or very short command lines for complex processes may indicate manual patching or evasion.

topics.title: DLL Analysis with dlllist and ldrmodules
topics.content: DLL analysis reveals what libraries a process has loaded, essential for detecting DLL injection and malicious module loading. The dlllist plugin walks the PEB InLoadOrderModuleList to show DLLs a process believes it has loaded. It displays base address, size, and full path for each DLL. Key analysis points: DLLs loaded from unusual paths (temp, appdata, downloads), missing legitimate system DLLs, DLLs with suspicious names or version info, and DLLs loaded but not in expected process. DLL injection techniques include LoadLibrary injection (DLL appears in lists), reflective DLL injection (DLL may not appear in standard lists), and DLL hollowing (legitimate DLL path but malicious code). For deeper analysis, use handles plugin to find open handles to DLL files, and malfind to detect injected code that may not appear as proper DLLs. Compare DLL lists between similar processes - all svchost.exe instances should have similar base DLLs loaded. Size anomalies may indicate patching or hollowing.

topics.title: Handle Analysis
topics.content: The handles plugin reveals kernel objects each process has open, including files, registry keys, mutexes, events, threads, and other processes. This is powerful for understanding process behavior and relationships. Handle analysis reveals: files being accessed or locked, registry keys being monitored or modified, inter-process communication via shared objects, mutexes used for single-instance enforcement (malware often creates unique mutexes), and process injection indicators (handles to other processes). Malware analysis: check for handles to sensitive files (SAM, SYSTEM hives), handles to lsass.exe from non-security processes, suspicious mutex names, and handles to remote process memory. Network-related handles may indicate network activity not visible in netscan. The output can be filtered by object type (File, Key, Process, Thread, Mutant, Event) to focus analysis. Large numbers of handles to system processes from user-mode applications may indicate malicious activity.

topics.title: Network Connection Analysis with netscan
topics.content: The netscan plugin extracts network connection information from memory, revealing active TCP connections, UDP endpoints, and listening sockets. Unlike live netstat which shows current connections, memory forensics captures point-in-time state that may include terminated connections still in memory. The output shows: local address and port, remote address and port (for TCP), connection state (ESTABLISHED, LISTENING, CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT, etc.), and owning process PID. This is critical for identifying command-and-control (C2) communications, data exfiltration, and lateral movement. Key analysis points: connections to external IPs from suspicious processes, high-numbered ephemeral ports (common for C2), connections from processes that shouldn't have network activity (notepad.exe, calc.exe), multiple connections to same IP from different processes, and connections to known-bad IPs (check against threat intelligence). UDP endpoints are particularly interesting as they may indicate DNS exfiltration or UDP-based C2. LISTENING ports reveal services that were available for exploitation. Compare netscan output with expected network behavior for the system role.

Some connections in CLOSE_WAIT or TIME_WAIT may be from legitimate terminated activity
IPv6 connections are often overlooked - check both TCPv4/TCPv6 and UDPv4/UDPv6
Port 443 doesn't guarantee HTTPS - malware often uses 443 to blend with normal traffic
best_practices: Cross-reference ForeignAddr with threat intelligence (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, internal TI)
Focus on connections from unexpected processes (notepad, calc, cmd/powershell to external IPs)
Check for high-numbered foreign ports (4444, 5555, 6666, 8080, 9999 - common C2)
Look for connections to internal IPs that may indicate lateral movement
Compare listening ports against expected services for the system
Document all external connections with timestamps for incident timeline

topics.title: Identifying Command and Control Communications
topics.content: Command and Control (C2) detection is a primary goal of memory forensics. Malware needs to communicate with attackers, and network artifacts in memory can reveal these channels. Key indicators: connections from unusual processes (notepad.exe, calc.exe, explorer.exe with external connections), connections to external IPs on suspicious ports (4444, 5555, 8080, 9999 are common C2 ports), multiple processes connecting to same external IP, beaconing patterns (regular interval connections), connections to IP addresses instead of domains, DNS over HTTPS artifacts, and connections to cloud services commonly abused (pastebin, discord, telegram). Combine netscan with process analysis: if PowerShell connects to an external IP, check cmdline for encoded commands. Correlate with timeline - C2 often established shortly after initial compromise. Check for proxy-aware malware by looking for connections to internal proxy servers. Some advanced malware uses DNS tunneling (look for DNS activity from non-system processes) or ICMP channels (harder to detect in memory). Cross-reference IPs with threat intelligence feeds for known-bad infrastructure.

[ANALYSIS NOTES]
- 185.234.67.89:4444 - Port 4444 is default Metasploit/Meterpreter - HIGH ALERT
- 185.234.67.89:8080 - Same IP different port - confirms C2 infrastructure
- notepad.exe with external connection - notepad should NEVER have network connections
- All connections established after 09:45 - matches incident timeline

warnings: C2 over HTTPS (port 443) is common and may look like legitimate traffic
Advanced malware may use Domain Fronting to hide C2 destination
DNS tunneling won't appear in netscan - check for unusual DNS process activity
Proxy-aware malware connects to internal proxy, not directly to C2
best_practices: Always correlate external IPs with threat intelligence
Focus on processes that shouldn't have network connections (notepad, calc, mspaint)
Check for beaconing by analyzing connection timestamps
Document all C2 indicators for IOC development and blocking
Cross-reference with cmdline to understand what commands C2 is executing
Use WHOIS and passive DNS to understand C2 infrastructure
